sec: Acute hepatitis · etiologies, HAV vs HEV features and serology

items.q: What is the most common clinical outcome of acute hepatitis?
items.exp: Under acute hepatitis outcomes, recovery is explicitly annotated with '(m/c)', followed by chronic hepatitis and rare fulminant failure. (Book p993)

items.q: Match each demographic group with the most common viral cause of acute hepatitis — 1) Children 2) Adults … A) Hepatitis E virus (HEV) B) Hepatitis A virus (HAV)
items.exp: Under viral causes of acute hepatitis, HAV is noted as '(m/c in children)' and HEV as '(m/c in adults)'. (Book p993)

items.q: Which of the following toxins is NOT listed under acute hepatitis causes on this page?
items.exp: The toxins listed are Rat poison (Yellow Phosphorus), Mushroom, and Alcohol; carbon tetrachloride is not among them. (Book p993)

items.q: Which two pharmaceutical classes are highlighted under the drug causes of acute hepatitis on this page?
items.exp: Under drug causes, the page lists Paracetamol and ATT (Anti-tubercular therapy). (Book p993)

items.q: Match each hepatitis virus with its taxonomic family and physical property — 1) Hepatitis A virus (HAV) 2) Hepatitis E virus (HEV) … A) Calicivirus family (Hepeviridae) with 4 genotypes B) Picornaviridae family; single-stranded RNA virus that is heat sensitive (>85°C)
items.exp: HAV belongs to Picornaviridae, is ssRNA and heat sensitive (>85°C); HEV belongs to the Calicivirus-like Hepeviridae family and has 4 genotypes. (Book p993)

items.q: What are the average incubation periods of Hepatitis A virus (HAV) and Hepatitis E virus (HEV)?
items.exp: In the comparison table, the incubation period is 30 days for HAV and 40 days for HEV. (Book p993)

items.q: Match each virus with its primary mechanism of hepatocellular injury — 1) Hepatitis A virus 2) Hepatitis E virus … A) Immune-mediated damage B) Direct cytopathic effect
items.exp: The table specifies the injury mechanism as 'Cytopathic effect' for HAV and 'Immune mediated' for HEV. (Book p993)

items.q: Assess the two statements comparing HAV and HEV: I Cholestatic hepatitis with prominent pruritus is rare in HAV but marked (+++) in HEV. II Hepatitis A frequently progresses to chronic carrier status in adults.
items.exp: Statement I is true because cholestatic hepatitis is rare in HAV and marked in HEV. Statement II is false because progression to chronicity is 'Not seen' in HAV. (Book p993)

items.q: A 10-year-old child presents with a 3-day prodrome of low-grade fever, nausea, and vomiting, followed by mild jaundice. Physical examination reveals tender hepatomegaly extending 1.5 cm below the costal margin and transient cutaneous lesions with joint pain. What is the most common extrahepatic feature of this infection?
items.exp: In HAV, tender hepatomegaly (max 2 cm) is found, and rash/arthralgia is explicitly annotated as the most common '(m/c)' extrahepatic feature. (Book p993)

items.q: Match each viral hepatitis with its characteristic diagnostic serology — 1) Acute Hepatitis A 2) Acute Hepatitis E … A) Anti-HEV IgM positive, which can persist up to 4 months B) Anti-HAV IgM positive with mixed pattern serum bilirubin elevation
items.exp: Acute HAV shows Anti-HAV IgM (+) with mixed bilirubin; acute HEV shows Anti-HEV IgM (+) that persists up to 4 months with conjugated bilirubin. (Book p993)

items.q: Fill up: In acute hepatitis E, the serum bilirubin characteristically exhibits a predominantly ______ pattern accompanied by prominent pruritus.
items.exp: Under lab investigations for HEV, serum bilirubin is specified as '(conjugated)' and accompanied by cholestatic pruritus. (Book p993)

items.q: Which of the following non-viral conditions is NOT listed under 'Others' as a cause of acute hepatitis?
items.exp: The 'Others' category lists Autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease, AFLP, and Budd-Chiari syndrome; hemochromatosis is a cause of chronic liver disease (p989). (Book p993)
